1.title: what the bread and the cup are doing
1.hook: a small square of bread and a tiny cup, passed down the row
1.tomorrow: the three names you say in one breath
1.howItsDone: Christians share bread and wine (or grape juice) as Jesus did at the last supper. Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at every Mass or Divine Liturgy; Protestant churches share it weekly, monthly or a few times a year, passed down the rows or received at the front; a few groups, such as Quakers, keep no outward meal.

segments.voice: A tray comes down the row. A small square of bread, or a thin wafer. Then a second tray, full of tiny cups: wine in some churches, grape juice in others. Some people eat right away. Some hold it and wait for everyone. Nobody stops to explain it, and somehow everybody knows what to do. All of it goes back to one dinner, on the night before Jesus died.
screen: `A TRAY COMES DOWN THE ROW.` → `BREAD. A TINY CUP.` → `ONE DINNER, THE NIGHT BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The night before he was executed, Jesus ate a Passover meal with his friends. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them: this is my body. Then the cup. Both times, one request: "this do in remembrance of me." Here's the surprise. Those words aren't only in the Gospels. A letter Paul wrote to a young church has them too, and it may be older than any Gospel. His word for remembrance is anamnesis, and many Christians hear more in it than a memory in the head: remembering with your hands, so the thing is present again. That's why the meal has more than one name. Communion means sharing: one loaf, many people. The Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks, what he did before he broke the bread. Some churches call it the Lord's Supper. And here churches honestly differ. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine. Many Protestant churches see them as signs, with the remembering at the heart. Others hold careful words of their own.

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Picture a table you've shared: a holiday, a kitchen, a last dinner before someone moved away. See one face at it. Breathe in. On the way out, let yourself remember them, not just think about them.
Communion. Sharing: one loaf, many people, and a meal that remembers. First word on your strand.

story.title: the dentist and the little cup
story.text: A dentist in New Jersey has a problem with the communion table. His Methodist church wants the meal without the alcohol, and grape juice won't stay juice: left alone, it turns into wine. In 1869, Thomas Welch tries a new idea from Louis Pasteur's work and heats the juice to stop it from fermenting. He offers it to churches as unfermented wine. They're slow to take it at first, but over the following decades the little cup of grape juice spreads through many Protestant churches.

2.title: the three names you say in one breath
2.hook: Father, Son and Holy Spirit: said at every baptism, rarely explained
2.tomorrow: the visitor who came at night
2.howItsDone: Many churches baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and many say the Nicene Creed, a statement of the Trinity, in their Sunday services; Catholic, Orthodox and some other Christians also make the sign of the cross with the same words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: communion, the meal that remembers. Today, three names many Christians say in a single breath.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It's said over a baby at a baptism, at the end of a service, with a hand moving forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder. Ask someone who has said it their whole life what it means, though, and you may get a long pause, and then a picture of a shamrock. First, a guess.
screen: `FATHER. SON. HOLY SPIRIT.` → `SAID A THOUSAND TIMES.` → `EXPLAINED?`

segments.voice: Christians say there is one God, and that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Three persons, one God. Not three gods. Not one God wearing three masks. The word Trinity isn't in the Bible. In the early 200s, a North African writer named Tertullian used the Latin trinitas to name something Christians saw all through the Gospels: Jesus praying to the Father, and promising to send the Spirit. At the end of one Gospel, he sends his friends out baptizing in the name, singular, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. One name. Three. Every easy picture breaks somewhere. Water, ice and steam make it one God changing forms, an idea early Christians turned down. A shamrock makes each person a third of God. So some teachers, as far back as Augustine, start somewhere else. One letter in the Bible says simply: God is love. And love needs someone to love. Many Christians hear the Trinity that way: at the very center of God, a relationship.
screen: `ONE GOD, THREE PERSONS.` · `THE WORD CAME LATER.` · `IN THE NAME — ONE NAME, THREE.` · `EVERY EASY PICTURE BREAKS.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in, and think of someone who loves you. Breathe out, and think of someone you love. Then notice the love between you: something real, though you can't hold it in your hand.
The Trinity. One God, three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Second word on your strand.

3.title: the visitor who came at night
3.hook: the altar call at camp, and a phrase that's older than any altar call
3.carry: never too old to start again
3.tomorrow: under the water and back up
3.howItsDone: Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians describe being born again as a moment of turning to Christ, sometimes at an altar call or by praying a short prayer; Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and other churches connect new birth closely with baptism and a lifelong turning toward God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Trinity, three and still one. Today, a phrase you've heard about people, and maybe about yourself.

The music slows down. Every head bowed, every eye closed. The speaker says: if you want to give your life to Jesus tonight, raise your hand, or come forward. Some people walked down that aisle at summer camp, some in a stadium, some never did. The phrase people used afterward was born again. That phrase is much older than any altar call. It comes from a conversation at night.

A respected teacher named Nicodemus comes to Jesus after dark. Jesus tells him: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word for again, anothen, has a second meaning: from above. Nicodemus hears the first one and asks the obvious question: "How can a man be born when he is old?" Climb back into the womb? Jesus means the second: a birth from above, by God's Spirit, which he compares to the wind. You can't see where it comes from; you only hear it. A few lines later comes the verse on the signs at football games, John 3:16: "For God so loved the world." The altar call itself is much newer. Revival preachers in the 1800s began inviting people to come forward, and big stadium crusades made it famous. Ask Jesus into your heart isn't a Bible phrase either; it's a simple way churches put it. And churches differ on how new birth happens: in a moment of decision, in baptism, over a lifetime. But notice the picture Jesus chose. Nobody gives birth to themselves.
screen: `A TEACHER, AFTER DARK.` · `ANOTHEN — AGAIN, FROM ABOVE.` · `LIKE THE WIND.` · `THE ALTAR CALL CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of something in your life that feels tired or stuck. On the second, notice you can't force it to be new, any more than a baby can give birth to itself. On the third, just leave a little room for something new to come.
Born again. In the Greek of the story, born from above, too. Third word.
Your line: never too old to start again. It answers the question Nicodemus asked that night. That's day three.

4.title: under the water and back up
4.hook: a baby in a white gown, a teenager in a pool: same word, an old disagreement
4.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize infants (by pouring, sprinkling or, in Orthodox churches, immersion); Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize believers, usually by full immersion. Almost all baptize once, in water, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: born again, born from above. Today, the water many churches tie to that new birth.

A baby in a long white gown, a little water poured over her head while the grandparents take photos. A teenager in a T-shirt, held by the shoulders and leaned back into a pool, coming up to cheering. Same word for both: baptism. Same faith. And a disagreement, centuries old, about when and how to do it. Both sides have their reasons.
screen: `A WHITE GOWN.` → `A T-SHIRT, A POOL.` → `SAME WORD.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse. It's older than the church. A wild preacher named John was dipping people in the Jordan River as a sign of turning their lives around, and Jesus himself walked into that river and was baptized. Later he sent his friends out to baptize, and from the start, baptism was how someone joined. So why two pictures? Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian churches baptize babies. The idea: God's promise comes first, before the child can answer, and the family promises to raise them in it. Baptist, Pentecostal and many non-denominational churches baptize people old enough to say yes for themselves, usually all the way under. Paul's picture fits that well: down into the water like a burial, up like rising from the dead. Whether baptism itself saves is a real difference too. Many churches call it the moment God makes a person new. Many others call it an outward sign of something God has already done inside. Either way, the shape is the same.

5.title: church words nobody defined
5.hook: quiet time, on fire, testimony: the church words you picked up like a family's inside jokes
5.howItsDone: Many evangelical churches, youth groups and camps invite people to share a testimony, the story of how they came to faith, aloud; many Christians also keep a daily quiet time of Bible reading and prayer, often in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: baptism, under the water and up again. Today, the words people used around it, the ones nobody ever looked up.

Quiet time. On fire for God. A hedge of protection. Traveling mercies. If you grew up in church, you probably learned these the way you learn a family's inside jokes: by hearing them a lot. People even have a name for it: Christianese. Today, three of them, and what's actually behind them.

Quiet time means a few minutes alone each day to read the Bible and pray. It has a model. One Gospel says Jesus got up "a great while before day" and went off to a solitary place to pray. On fire means eager, all in. It echoes two friends on a road who said, after a stranger turned out to be Jesus, that their hearts had burned inside them while he talked. And testimony. At camp or youth group, someone stands by the bonfire and tells how they came to faith. Testimony is a courtroom word. In Greek it's martyria, from martys: a witness, someone who says what they saw. Early Christians who died rather than take back what they'd witnessed were called by that same word, and it came into English as martyr. So a testimony isn't a performance, and it isn't a sales pitch. It's a witness statement: here's what happened to me. Some people love telling theirs to a crowd. Plenty of Christians keep theirs for a friend, or for nobody but God.
screen: `QUIET TIME — A HABIT OF JESUS.` · `ON FIRE — A BURNING HEART.` · `TESTIMONY — A WITNESS.` · `MARTYS — WITNESS, THEN MARTYR.`

Testimony. From the Greek for witness: here's what I saw happen. Fifth word.

6.title: wind, breath and fire
6.hook: the third name nobody explained, and what speaking in tongues is
6.tomorrow: a library that tells one story
6.howItsDone: Christians pray to and through the Holy Spirit and celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter; in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, speaking in tongues, healing prayer and prophecy are part of worship, while many other churches pray more quietly for the Spirit's gifts and fruit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: testimony, a witness statement. Today, the third name in the blessing from day two.

Of the three names, Father and Son come with pictures. The Holy Spirit can feel like the one nobody explained. Maybe you saw people speaking in tongues at a friend's church and wondered what was happening. Maybe you wondered why it never happened to you. The words underneath are plainer than you'd think: breath, and wind.

In Hebrew the word is ruach; in Greek, pneuma. Both mean breath, wind and spirit, all at once. On the Bible's first page, the spirit of God, or the wind of God, moves over the waters. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says: receive the Holy Spirit. Jesus calls the Spirit the Paraclete: the one called alongside you. A helper, an advocate, someone in your corner. Then fire. Fifty days after Passover, at the festival of Pentecost, his friends hear a sound like a rushing wind, something like flames rests on each of them, and they speak in languages the visiting crowd can understand. Speaking in tongues today is understood in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic churches treasure it as a living gift, often as a way of praying. Some churches believe that gift belonged mainly to the first generation; many others are open to it but rarely practice it. And Paul, writing to a church that prized it, asks: "do all speak with tongues?" He expects the answer no. His list of what the Spirit grows is quieter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness.

7.hook: not one book but a shelf of them, read as one story from a garden to a city
7.tomorrow: you've said it a thousand times
7.howItsDone: Christians read the Bible aloud in church services, often from both Testaments, and many read it at home through a daily plan or an app; churches differ on which books belong in the Old Testament (66 books in Protestant Bibles, 73 in Catholic, more in Orthodox).

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Holy Spirit, breath and wind and fire. Six words so far: communion, the Trinity, born again, baptism, testimony, the Holy Spirit. Today, the seventh, where all of them come from.
screen: `COMMUNION · TRINITY · BORN AGAIN · BAPTISM · TESTIMONY · HOLY SPIRIT`

segments.voice: It's in a hotel drawer, on a phone app, in a grandmother's lap with the pages gone soft. It's easy to picture one thick book. Open the table of contents, though, and it's a whole shelf: poems, letters, laws, family stories, songs of complaint, four lives of Jesus. Written over many centuries, by many hands. And Christians read it as one story.
screen: `A HOTEL DRAWER. A PHONE.` → `ONE BOOK?` → `A WHOLE SHELF.`

segments.voice: The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia: the books. Plural. A library. If you've ever started on page one and gotten lost somewhere in the laws, that's why: nobody reads a library front to back, and a lot of people start with one of the Gospels instead. Protestant Bibles have sixty-six books, Catholic Bibles seventy-three, Orthodox Bibles a few more. There are two big parts. The Old Testament is the Jewish scriptures, the ones Jesus himself read. The New Testament was written by his first followers. Testament means covenant: a binding promise. Here's a surprise. The chapter and verse numbers aren't original. Chapters came in the 1200s, and the New Testament's verse numbers in the 1500s, so for most of Christian history nobody could look up day three's verse as John 3:16. Then the shape. Many Christians tell it in a few big moves: a world made good, a family chosen, slaves set free, kings and prophets, exile and return, then Jesus, and his followers sent out. And the bookends. Near the very start there's a garden with a tree of life. On the last page, the tree of life is back, growing beside a river in a city made new. The story ends where it began.
screen: `TA BIBLIA — THE BOOKS.` · `TESTAMENT — A PROMISE.` · `THE NUMBERS CAME LATER.` · `A GARDEN, THEN A CITY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of where your own story started. On the second, think of a chapter that was hard. On the third, picture one thing you hope gets made new. Three breaths, one story.
The Bible. Ta biblia, the books: a library Christians read as one story. Seventh word, and a week's worth.
Your line: one story, many books. That's week one: seven words, all from that one shelf. Tomorrow, a word you've said a thousand times.

what a scholar hears: ta biblia, 'the books'; chapters by Stephen Langton (c. 1227), New Testament verse numbers by Robert Estienne (1551); canons of 66 (Protestant), 73 (Catholic) and more (Orthodox).

story.title: the scroll in the rubble
story.text: Workers repairing the temple in Jerusalem find a scroll nobody remembers. The high priest hands it to the king's secretary, who reads it aloud to the young king, Josiah. As he listens, the king tears his clothes: his people have forgotten what's written there. He gathers everyone, from the greatest to the least, and has the whole book read out loud to them.

wrong.myth: the Bible is one book, written all at once.
wrong.truth: it's a library: sixty-six books in Protestant Bibles, more in Catholic and Orthodox ones, written over many centuries.
